stimulus: Hysteresis loops are the first thing anyone draws, and they're a little deceptive, because a loop only says the present depends on the past, not that anything is being kept. A slow-relaxing paramagnet can fake it if you sweep fast enough. So people start varying the sweep rate, and the loop's width changes, which is a clue that time matters, that "memory" is partly just sluggishness. Then there's the first-order reversal curve trick: climb partway up, come back down, map the whole family of little returns, and suddenly you see a Preisach plane, a census of tiny bistable switches, each with its own up-threshold and down-threshold. Memory as a crowd of cheap two-state units. That reminds me of return-point memory, where the material remembers the extremum of a history even after being wiggled inside it, like wiping out a cache only when you exceed the old peak. Barkhausen noise: you can hear domain walls snapping, pinned on defects, crackling like a fire. The memory is literally in the dirt, the pinning sites. Demagnetize with an AC field decaying slowly and the record vanishes, which is how you test erasure. Spin glasses do something stranger: age them, and they remember temperature pauses as dips in the curve. Old tape drifts, print-through bleeds between layers on a reel. Thermal stability of a hard drive bit gets a number, the KV over kT ratio, and everyone argues about ten years versus a century.

Research question: "What analyses or measurements would best test whether AP-1 acts as a cellular memory mechanism?"

Propose 5 distinct, concrete ideas (analyses, measurements, or experiments) that a research lab could pursue to address this question. For each idea give a short title and a description of one or two sentences.

ideas.title: Sweep-rate and relaxation controls for AP-1 hysteresis
ideas.description: Stimulate cells with graded, ramped doses of a signal (e.g., TPA, EGF, or anisomycin) up and down at several sweep rates, then read out AP-1 activity (FOS/JUN levels, a reporter, ATAC accessibility at AP-1 motifs). If loop width shrinks as the sweep slows, the apparent memory is just slow relaxation. If it persists at slow rates, it reflects a bistable or stored state. Add the same sweep to a JUN/FOS degradation-rate mutant to separate sluggish kinetics from true retention.

ideas.title: First-order reversal curve mapping of single-cell AP-1 thresholds
ideas.description: Drive cells partway up the dose axis, reverse, and repeat from many reversal points. Use live single-cell AP-1 reporters or multiplexed imaging to build a Preisach-like distribution of up- and down-switching thresholds across cells. A population of bistable cells with distinct thresholds would support a memory made of many two-state units, while a unimodal graded response would argue against it.

ideas.title: Return-point and erasure tests with decaying-oscillation stimulation
ideas.description: Give a pulse history with a defined peak, wiggle the stimulus inside that peak, and check whether AP-1 target gene output and chromatin state remember only the maximum, as in return-point memory. Test erasure by applying a slowly decaying oscillating stimulus or an inhibitor wash-out (e.g., a dominant-negative FOS such as A-FOS), and measure how much stimulus is needed to wipe the record. Compare the dose needed to erase with the dose needed to write.

ideas.title: Locating the pinning sites: AP-1 binding, chromatin, and mutation at the enhancer level
ideas.description: Map where memory is stored using CUT&RUN or ChIP for FOS/JUN, ATAC-seq, and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) at sites before, during, and after the stimulus. Then use CRISPR to mutate individual AP-1 motifs or degrade AP-1 with a degron after the stimulus, and ask whether enhancer accessibility and the response to a second stimulus persist without AP-1. This distinguishes memory held in AP-1 itself, in feedback loops, or in chromatin sites that AP-1 only opened (like defects holding domain walls).

ideas.title: Aging and pause-memory tests, with stability quantified
ideas.description: Vary the interval between the first and second stimulus (minutes to weeks) and the number of cell divisions between them, using single-cell tracking to see whether the second response is primed. Insert interruptions (e.g., a temporary signaling block mid-history) to see if cells recall them as dips in later response. Fit the decay to extract a retention half-life and an energy-barrier-like parameter, to say whether AP-1 memory lasts hours, days or generations.
